title: Yajnavalkya and his two wives: he's leaving (2.4)
hook: the greatest sage in the book tells his wife he's leaving home for good, and offers to split the property
tomorrow: Maitreyi: "what would I do with wealth if it doesn't make me immortal?"

segments.voice: Yesterday, priya: the self is dearer than a son, because it is more inward. Your line was love the self. Did you notice where your love was coming from? Day three hundred sixty-six.

A kitchen, a long marriage, an ordinary evening. And the husband says: I'm going. Not to another house. Not to another person. He's leaving the life of a householder altogether, to wander with nothing. Before I go, he says, let me divide what I have between you and my other wife, so it's settled. That's how one of the Brihadaranyaka's great conversations begins. The man is Yajnavalkya, and today is about him, and about what it meant, in his world, to leave.
screen: `I'M GOING.` → `NOT TO ANOTHER HOUSE.` → `LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya is a leading voice of this Upanishad. Tradition credits him with a whole branch of the Veda, the White Yajurveda, and in a few days you'll watch him take on a room full of rivals. Here he's at home. He has two wives. Maitreyi and Katyayani. That's nearly all the text tells us about them in this chapter. When the same scene is told again, later in the book, it adds one line: Maitreyi was one who discussed Brahman, and Katyayani had, in the text's short phrase, a woman's knowledge, words readers interpret in different ways. And that's it. The text never tells us what Katyayani thought, or how either of them felt. It's silent, and it's fair to say so. Why is he leaving? Hindu tradition later described life in four stages: the student, the householder, the forest dweller, and the renunciant, the sannyasi, who gives up home, property and name, and wanders. Yajnavalkya is stepping from the second stage toward the last. When the scene is retold, the verb is the one used for going forth into that wandering life. And notice what he does first. He doesn't vanish in the night. He sits down and tries to settle the property fairly. Even leaving everything, he wants to leave well. One more thing: this whole conversation appears twice in the Brihadaranyaka, in book two and again in book four, with small differences. The book keeps both tellings. And what keeps the scene alive is what Maitreyi says next.
screen: `A LEADING VOICE OF THIS UPANISHAD.` · `TWO WIVES; THE TEXT SAYS LITTLE MORE.` · `FROM HOUSEHOLDER TO WANDERER.` · `TOLD TWICE IN THE SAME BOOK.` · then, large: `THE MAN WHO LEFT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes on leaving well. Sit, and breathe. Think of something you're getting ready to leave, or will one day: a job, a house, a role, a habit, a stage of life. Don't decide anything. Just ask what Yajnavalkya asked: what would it take to settle this fairly, so the people around it are cared for? Let one small answer come. Then let the question go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sannyasa, renunciation, laying everything down. He is leaving home for good, and first offers to settle his property between Maitreyi and Katyayani.
Your line: the man who left. Today, finish one thing properly before you walk away from it: a conversation, a task, a goodbye. Day three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition sannyasa is taken by formal vows, often late in life, after which the renunciant leaves home and property behind; the four stages of life are an ideal pattern described in the dharma texts, and the householder's life is honored in its own right.

fork.setup: you're a householder who has decided to go forth and wander with nothing. you have two wives and some property. what do you do first?
options: sit down and settle the property between them.
give it all to the priests.
fork.reveal: Yajnavalkya offers to make a settlement between Maitreyi and Katyayani. then Maitreyi asks a question that changes the whole conversation.

original.note: Sanskrit saṃnyāsa: laying everything down. the fourth and last stage of life in the dharma texts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man walking out on his family.
what it means: Yajnavalkya is going forth as a wandering renunciant, and settles his property first.
what a scholar hears: the scene is told twice (2.4 and 4.5). only the second telling describes the wives, and uses the verb for going forth into the wandering life.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.5.1–2 (the retelling: Maitreyi a discusser of Brahman; 'about to go forth')

notes: 4.5.1 describes Maitreyi as brahmavādinī and Katyayani as strīprajñā; rendered gently as 'the knowledge most women of her day had'. A Keeper may prefer different wording.
2.4.1 uses udyāsyan (going up/away from this state); 4.5.2 uses pravrajiṣyan (about to go forth as a renunciant). Confirm.
Tradition credits Yajnavalkya with the White (Shukla) Yajurveda; confirm phrasing.
The four ashramas are a later dharma-text scheme; the script says 'Hindu tradition later described'. Confirm.

Review (2026-10-01): word segment now speaks the index word (it said 'Sannyasa'); 'most famous conversation' and 'the great voice' softened; 'the knowledge most women of her day had' (an uncited generalization) replaced by the text's own phrase, stri-prajna, noted as variously read; 'almost word for word' overstated the match of 2.4 and 4.5, now 'with small differences'; Katyayani no longer called 'the second wife' (the text gives no order).
